summaries.example: Imagine a machine that helps plan a trip. An analog machine might use a moving needle to show speed, like a car's speedometer. A digital machine would use written symbols, such as 0 and 1, to store numbers and instructions. A stored-program computer could keep the trip instructions in its memory and follow them in order.
summaries.summary: The history of computing did not begin with laptops. It began with human calculators and machines that followed reliable steps. Charles Babbage designed mechanical digital engines. His Difference Engine was meant to produce useful mathematical tables. His more ambitious Analytical Engine was planned with memory, a calculating part, and punched-card instructions. Ada Lovelace understood that such a machine might work with more than numbers, including music. Early machines also used analog methods, representing one thing with a changing physical feature such as an angle or voltage. In 1936, Alan Turing described a universal machine: a machine with memory that could read symbols, write symbols, and follow instructions stored in that memory. During and after the Second World War, engineers built faster machines with relays and then vacuum tubes. Colossus was an important electronic machine used for codebreaking, though it was special-purpose and did not store its programs internally. ENIAC was another large electronic machine, built for calculating artillery tables, but it too had to be rewired for new tasks. The Manchester Baby, ACE, EDVAC, and other projects moved toward stored-program computers. New memory technologies, including delay lines, cathode-ray-tube storage, drums, and magnetic core, made computers more practical.
key_ideas: Computing began with people who calculated by following repeatable methods.
Charles Babbage planned mechanical machines, including one for making mathematical tables and another designed to be general-purpose.
Analog machines used changing physical features, while digital machines used symbols and numbers.
Alan Turing described a universal machine with memory, a scanner, and stored instructions.
Electronic parts such as vacuum tubes worked much faster than machines using mechanical relays.
Early computers such as Colossus, the Manchester Baby, ENIAC, and EDVAC helped develop modern computing.
summaries.why_it_matters: This history shows that computers grew from many kinds of ideas. Mechanical design, mathematics, electronics, memory, and programming all mattered. It also shows why a computer is more than a fast calculator: a general-purpose machine can keep instructions, change what it does, and handle many kinds of problems.

important_terms.definition: A person who carries out calculations by following clear steps. Before electronic machines, many people did this work.
A machine that represents something by copying one of its changing features, such as using voltage to represent speed.
A machine that represents information with separate symbols, especially 0 and 1.
A computer idea in which both information and the instructions for working on it are kept in memory.
A method for choosing a different next instruction when a condition is true, such as taking a different path in a game.
A kind of memory that kept pulses moving through a tube, so information could be read again later.

summaries.example: Suppose two machines must solve a changing set of equations. An analog machine could represent a variable through an electrical voltage and connect components that perform operations in parallel. This may be fast, but changing the problem can require substantial hardware adjustment, and greater precision is costly. A digital stored-program machine instead encodes numbers and instructions as symbols, allowing a program in memory to direct operations and branch when a test gives a particular result.
summaries.summary: The entry traces a change in both machines and concepts. Originally, “computers” were human clerks who followed effective methods. Later, computing machines performed similar work mechanically, electromechanically, or electronically. Babbage's Difference Engine was a special-purpose digital machine intended to produce mathematical tables. His Analytical Engine was more significant conceptually: it was planned as a general-purpose digital machine with a store, a calculating “mill,” punched-card instructions, and conditional branching. Ada Lovelace recognized that its possible operations need not be limited to numerical calculation. Analog computers represented quantities through corresponding physical properties, such as shaft angles or electrical potentials. They could solve systems of operations in parallel, but adapting them to new problems and increasing precision could be difficult. Digital machines represented information discretely. Turing's 1936 universal machine gave a powerful abstract account of a machine with unlimited memory, a scanner, and instructions stored as symbols. This stored-program concept became central to postwar computer design. Relays enabled early digital machines but were relatively slow. Vacuum tubes made large-scale electronic computation much faster. Colossus demonstrated the power of electronic digital processing in codebreaking, yet it was special-purpose and configured through physical controls. ENIAC likewise required rewiring. Projects associated with Turing, Newman, Williams, Kilburn, Eckert, Mauchly, and von Neumann helped move computing toward general-purpose stored-program systems. key_ideas: The meaning of 'computer' shifted from a human calculator to a machine carrying out effective procedures.
Babbage's Analytical Engine anticipated major components of general-purpose computing: memory, a calculating unit, programs, and conditional control.
Analog and digital computation differ in how representation relates to what is represented, not merely in whether a machine is old or new.
Turing's universal-machine description supplied a conceptual model for stored programs and general-purpose computation.
The transition from relays to vacuum tubes increased speed, while machines such as Colossus and ENIAC still lacked internally stored programs.
The early history involved both abstract contributions and engineering work; no single person or machine explains the emergence of modern computers.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry matters because it connects philosophical questions about computation with concrete engineering history. It clarifies that computation involves representations, rules, memory, and control—not simply electronic speed. It also complicates simple “inventor” stories: Babbage and Turing supplied influential conceptual frameworks, while many engineers made those frameworks work under practical constraints. The development of memory and stored programs changed machines from devices built for particular calculations into systems capable of running varied procedures.

important_terms.definition: A representation in which some physical feature of the representing system corresponds to a feature of what is represented; for example, voltage may represent speed.
A representation using discrete symbols, historically often binary digits, rather than a continuously varying physical magnitude.
The idea that a machine stores its instructions in the same memory system as its data, allowing instructions to be read and potentially altered during operation.
A machine description with a memory, a symbol-reading and writing mechanism, and instructions determining its successive actions.
A rule-of-thumb strategy that reduces the amount of searching needed to find a solution; Turing connected such methods with possible machine intelligence.
A machine whose physical arrangement or wiring determines its task, rather than a stored internal program selecting the task.
A memory method using magnetic materials arranged so that stored information can be reached without waiting for it to travel through a fixed sequence.

summaries.example: Think about a school robot that solves puzzles. If its wires must be rearranged for every new puzzle, it is being set up for each task. If the puzzle-solving instructions are stored inside its memory, the robot can use one machine for many puzzles. It might even test a condition—such as whether a path is blocked—and choose a different instruction.
summaries.summary: Computing has a longer history than electronic computers. The word once described human workers who performed calculations by following dependable methods. Charles Babbage designed mechanical digital machines. His Difference Engine was meant to produce tables used in mathematics, astronomy, tides, and other work. His Analytical Engine was a much broader plan. It included a memory, a calculating unit, and punched-card instructions. It was also supposed to choose among actions based on earlier results. Ada Lovelace saw that such a machine might be used for tasks beyond ordinary arithmetic. Another important path was analog computing. An analog representation uses a physical feature that varies in a way related to the thing represented. A digital representation uses separate symbols. In 1936, Alan Turing described a universal machine with memory, a scanner, and stored instructions. This led to the stored-program idea: data and instructions could be held in memory, making a machine easier to use for many different tasks. Early digital computers often used relays, which were mechanical switches driven by electricity. Vacuum tubes were faster because they did not depend on moving mechanical parts. During the Second World War, Colossus used electronic processing for codebreaking. It was important but special-purpose, and operators set it up with switches and plugs. ENIAC, completed in the United States in 1945, was another large electronic machine; it was designed mainly for artillery calculations and also needed physical reconfiguration for new jobs. Later projects, including the Manchester Baby, Turing's ACE, and EDVAC, developed stored-program computing. Advances in memory—such as delay lines, cathode-ray tubes, drums, and magnetic core—were essential to this progress.
key_ideas: The word computer first referred to people and later became the name for machines.
Babbage's designs show that important computer ideas appeared before electronics.
Analog and digital machines use different ways to represent information.
Turing's abstract machine explained how memory and instructions could make one machine capable of many tasks.
Relays, vacuum tubes, and new memory systems each shaped what early computers could do.
Colossus and ENIAC were powerful electronic machines, but they were not full stored-program general-purpose computers.
summaries.why_it_matters: This story explains why modern computers can perform many unrelated jobs. The crucial change was not only replacing gears with electronics. It was combining representations, memory, instructions, and control. The history also teaches that inventions develop through cooperation and disagreement: theoretical models, practical machines, and new memory technologies influenced one another.

important_terms.definition: A person whose job was to perform calculations by using a reliable series of steps.
A machine that represents a quantity through a matching physical change, such as a voltage representing speed.
A machine that uses separate symbols or digits, commonly including 0 and 1, to represent information.
A design in which instructions are kept in memory along with data, so the machine can follow a program without being rewired.
A choice in a program: if a test has one result, follow one instruction; otherwise, follow another.
An electronic component with no moving mechanical parts that was used to make early computers much faster than relay-based machines.
A practical strategy that helps narrow a search for a solution without checking every possibility.
